t: Cultural Inscriptions in the Hymns of Anonymous Sangam Poets
x: <jats:p>Among the languages of the world, Tamil is hailed as the supreme classical language. Tamil is an ancient, classical, and prosperous language. Literature is one factor that enriches the language. In the Sangam society, which was centred on human life, honour for men and chastity for women became ornaments. People lived a cultured life where they lived and let others live. They accepted married life in the community wholeheartedly. Hospitality was prized as the chief virtue. The author names of many hymns are unknown in the Sangam literature, ‘Ettuthogai’, which is such a cultural treasury and primary literature. This research explores the richness of cultural richness, lifestyles, and beliefs found in the songs of anonymous poets.</jats:p>

x: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:p>Ideally, an epigraphist should study and edit an inscription from the original stone, copper plate, or other surface on which it is written. In practice, however, this is often not practically feasible, so that the editor must rely on some means of reproduction of the original. Of course, even if one does have access to the original, a reproduction should be made for future use and for publication, since a published edition of an inscription should include a good illustration of the original along with the edited transcript, to enable the readers to check the editor’s readings.</jats:p>

t: <p>Tamil Words in Early Prakrit Inscriptions in Sri Lanka</p>
x: <jats:p><span>Early Prakrit inscriptions in Sri Lanka (c. 2nd century BC–2nd century AD) contain several terms of Tamil origin, including Parumaka, Veḷ, maḷa, and marumakaṉ. Analysis of their phonological and morphological features—such as retroflex consonants and Dravidian suffixes—suggests these are Prakritized forms of Tamil chieftain and kinship terms. Their presence in the earliest inscriptions indicates a Dravidian linguistic substrate and reflects the incorporation of Tamil speaking populations into the formation of early Sinhala society.</span></jats:p>

Chola (Cola) Empire
x: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>The Chola Empire was established in South India in the 9th century and flourished for almost 400 years. Its territorial extent, military strength, institutional structures, and monumental art attest to the power and authority of the dynasty. Starting from modest origins in the fertile uplands along the Kaveri River, the Cholas first extended and consolidated their rule over the entire Tamil macro‐region. Thereafter, they brought contiguous regions as well as far off places under their sway. In the annals of Indian history, the imperial grandeur of the Cholas remains an important reference point to assess the sociopolitical and economic institutions in the premodern period.</jats:p>
